newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Wildlife groups say climate change threatens parks.
newsitem.headline: Wildlife groups say climate change threatens parks.

text.p: Dwindling wildlife species that have found refuge in U.S. and Canadian national parks face a new threat -- global warming -- wildlife advocates said on Tuesday.

In a report released at the U.N. Earth Summit, the World Wildlife Fund for Nature (WWF) said many national parks and wildlife refuges are already are showing effects of warmer temperatures and more severe weather, particularly in northern Canada, Alaska and along the coasts.

If unchecked, the WWF report said, global warming will drastically change vegetation in more than 25 percent of U.S. national parks and will destroy wetlands in the U.S. Upper Midwest which are breeding grounds for migratory birds.
Individual parks that are particularly threatened include Yellowstone, Yosemite, the Everglades, the Great Smoky Mountains, Hawaii's Haleakala, and Alaska's Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, it said.
U.S. Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt called the report a "wake-up call" and said even if just a part of its warnings came true, parks would be harmed.

"Climate change may seem a long way off, and perhaps too uncertain to concern those of us who manage parks and other public lands. This report released today points out the folly of doing so," Babbitt said in a statement.

The report cited examples of rapidly shrinking glaciers at Glacier National Park, melting permafrost in Alaska, and rising sea levels in coastal wetlands such as Maryland's Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge.
Warmer temperatures will redistribute plant species and change wildlife habitat, harming many creatures whose survival depends on a delicate interplay of climate and food, it said.
For example, it said warmer, drier conditions would reduce grizzly bear habitat in Yellowstone National Park by as much as 90 percent within 50 years.

In Alaska, the report said melting permafrost and the loss of tundra ecosystems threatened caribou and other wildlife in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, and melting sea ice threatened polar bears.
Warmer conditions also will lead to more forest fires, invasive plant and insect species and drought, damaging or altering most forests and refuges, it said.

Even if nations agreed to take immediate steps to reduce fossil fuel pollution that is heating the atmosphere, the report said some climate changes would occur and parks should be managed to adjust to this.
"Climate change will force the need for the most resilient protected area system we can create, and this in turn will require increased investment in conservation," the WWF said.

"The current protected area system, although it will be extremely hard hit by global warming, can provide the core habitat needed for species survival if more is done to promote conservation in areas surrounding the parks."
